title: Intrusive Thoughts: Why You Have Them and What to Do
description: Disturbing thoughts don't mean you're a bad person. Understanding intrusive thoughts, why they stick, and how to stop them from controlling your life.

content.text: What if I hurt someone? What if I'm a pedophile? What if I don't really love my partner? These terrifying thoughts are intrusive thoughts—and they're more common than you think.
Intrusive thoughts are unwanted, involuntary thoughts, images, or urges that pop into your mind. Everyone has them—research shows 90%+ of people experience intrusive thoughts.

items: Violence: Thoughts of harming others or yourself
Sexual: Unwanted sexual thoughts, including about children or inappropriate people
Relationship: Doubts about love, attraction, fidelity
Religious/blasphemous: Thoughts violating your values
Contamination: Fear of germs, illness, contamination
Harm: Fear you'll cause accidents or harm through negligence

content.text: The thought isn't the problem—your reaction is. When you:

items: Try to suppress the thought (makes it stronger)
Analyze it ('What does this mean about me?')
Seek reassurance ('I would never do that, right?')
Do mental or physical rituals to neutralize it
Avoid situations that trigger it

content.text: ...you teach your brain this thought is important and dangerous. It comes back stronger.
The fact that these thoughts disturb you proves they're NOT desires. People who actually want to act on violent or inappropriate urges don't feel tortured by the thoughts.

items: They cause significant distress
You spend 1+ hours daily on thoughts or responses to them
They interfere with work, relationships, or daily life
You do mental or physical compulsions to manage them

content.text: The gold standard treatment. You deliberately expose yourself to triggers while resisting compulsions. Counterintuitive but highly effective.

items: Analyzing the thoughts
Seeking reassurance
Trying to stop thinking them
Talk therapy that explores 'meaning' of thoughts
Avoiding triggers
Notice the thought without engaging: 'There's that thought again'
Don't argue with it or analyze it
Accept uncertainty: 'Maybe I'm a bad person, maybe I'm not'
Keep doing what you were doing
See an OCD specialist if it's affecting your life

content.text: Intrusive thoughts are normal—even disturbing ones. What matters is how you respond. Fighting them makes them stronger. Accepting them as brain noise and continuing with life weakens them. If they're taking over, ERP therapy can help.
